sec.t:
बड़ी संख्याएँ मॉडल से आसानी से समझ आती हैं। अगर धरती एक मटर का दाना हो, तो बृहस्पति एक मौसंबी होगा और सूरज रसोई की मेज़ से भी ऊँचा। ऐसे [[@big-small-scale|पैमाने वाले मॉडल]] दिखाते हैं कि बृहस्पति ग्रहों का सरदार क्यों है।

उसका [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] भी ताक़तवर है। अगर तुम उसके बादलों के ऊपर खड़े हो पाते, तो तुम्हारा वज़न धरती से लगभग ढाई गुना होता। घर पर 30 किलो का बच्चा वहाँ 75 किलो जैसा महसूस करेगा।

फिर भी यह दस घंटे से कम में एक चक्कर घूम जाता है। इस तेज़ घुमाव से बृहस्पति बीच से फूल जाता है, इसलिए वह ध्रुव से ध्रुव तक के मुकाबले अपनी [[equator|भूमध्य रेखा]] पर साफ़ तौर पर ज़्यादा चौड़ा है।

बृहस्पति की सबसे मशहूर चीज़ एक विशाल तूफ़ान है, जिसे महान लाल धब्बा कहते हैं। 1830 के दशक से इस पर लगातार नज़र रखी जा रही है, और यह शायद उससे भी बहुत पुराना है। इसकी हवाएँ सैकड़ों किलोमीटर प्रति घंटा की रफ़्तार से चलती हैं।

सौ साल पहले यह धब्बा इतना चौड़ा था कि उसमें लगभग तीन धरतियाँ समा जातीं। यह सिकुड़ता जा रहा है, और आज यह एक धरती से बस थोड़ा ही ज़्यादा चौड़ा है। कोई नहीं जानता कि यह किसी दिन ग़ायब हो जाएगा या नहीं।

जुलाई 1994 में दुनिया भर के लोगों ने एक धूमकेतु को बृहस्पति से टकराते देखा। बृहस्पति के गुरुत्वाकर्षण ने [[@comets-famous|शूमेकर-लेवी 9 धूमकेतु]] को 20 से ज़्यादा टुकड़ों में तोड़ दिया था। एक के बाद एक ये टुकड़े ग्रह के बादलों में जा धँसे। उनके छोड़े काले निशान धरती से भी बड़े थे और हफ़्तों तक बने रहे।

बृहस्पति का गुरुत्वाकर्षण पास से गुज़रते [[@comets|धूमकेतुओं]] और [[asteroid|क्षुद्रग्रहों]] को हमेशा खींचता रहता है। कुछ वैज्ञानिक मानते हैं कि इससे धरती बचती है, क्योंकि बृहस्पति उन्हें बुहार लेता है। दूसरे कहते हैं कि बृहस्पति उन्हें अंदर वाले ग्रहों की ओर उछाल भी सकता है। सच शायद दोनों का थोड़ा-थोड़ा है।

कई अंतरिक्ष यान बृहस्पति के पास से गुज़रे हैं, जिनमें 1979 में दोनों वॉयजर यान भी थे, जिन्होंने उसके धुंधले छल्ले खोजे। नासा का जूनो यान 2016 में पहुँचा और तब से उसके ध्रुवों के ऊपर चक्कर लगा रहा है। उसने ऐसे घुमावदार तूफ़ान देखे हैं जो किसी चित्रकारी जैसे लगते हैं। यूरोपीय अंतरिक्ष एजेंसी का JUICE और नासा का यूरोपा क्लिपर उसके बर्फ़ीले चंद्रमाओं का अध्ययन करने के लिए रास्ते में हैं।

हम इसे बृहस्पति या गुरु कहते हैं, और इसी के नाम पर हफ़्ते का एक दिन है, बृहस्पतिवार या गुरुवार। चाँद और [[@venus-hot|शुक्र]] के बाद यह अक्सर रात के आसमान का सबसे चमकीला बिंदु होता है। आम [[@stargazing|दूरबीन]] को स्थिर पकड़कर देखो, तो कभी-कभी गैलीलियो के चारों चंद्रमा एक कतार में नन्हे बिंदुओं जैसे दिख जाते हैं।

text: शनि के छल्ले बर्फ़ के अरबों टुकड़ों से बने हैं, जिनमें थोड़ी चट्टान और धूल भी मिली है। कुछ टुकड़े चीनी के दानों जितने छोटे हैं। कुछ एक घर जितने बड़े। हर टुकड़ा अपनी अलग राह पर शनि का चक्कर लगाता है, एक नन्हे चंद्रमा की तरह।

दूर से ये टुकड़े आपस में धुंधलाकर ठोस पट्टियों जैसे दिखते हैं। ये पट्टियाँ चौड़ी तो हैं, पर हैरान कर देने वाली हद तक पतली। मुख्य छल्ले एक किनारे से दूसरे किनारे तक लगभग 2,80,000 किलोमीटर तक फैले हैं, धरती से चाँद की दूरी के दो-तिहाई से भी ज़्यादा। फिर भी ज़्यादातर जगहों पर ये बस लगभग 10 मीटर मोटे हैं, मोटे तौर पर एक तीन मंज़िला इमारत की ऊँचाई जितने।

बर्फ़ धूप को अच्छे से लौटाती है, इसीलिए शनि के छल्ले इतनी आसानी से दिखते हैं, एक छोटी-सी [[@telescopes-how|दूरबीन]] से भी। छल्ले रोशनी को कैसे लौटाते हैं, इसका अध्ययन करके वैज्ञानिकों ने पता लगाया है कि वे ज़्यादातर पानी की बर्फ़ से बने हैं, और उनमें गहरे रंग की धूल बस ज़रा-सी छिड़की हुई है।

[[@jupiter-giant|बृहस्पति]], [[@uranus-sideways|यूरेनस]] और [[@neptune-winds|नेपच्यून]] के छल्लों की कहानी अलग है। वे ज़्यादातर गहरे रंग की धूल और चट्टानी टुकड़ों से बने हैं, और बहुत कम रोशनी लौटाते हैं। इसीलिए 300 से ज़्यादा सालों तक शनि ही इकलौता छल्लों वाला ग्रह माना जाता रहा।

1610 में जब [[@galileo|गैलीलियो]] ने अपनी शुरुआती [[telescope|दूरबीन]] शनि की ओर की, तो उन्हें कुछ अजीब दिखा। ग्रह के दोनों ओर दो उभार लग रहे थे, कानों जैसे, या कप के हत्थों जैसे। दो साल बाद ये "कान" ग़ायब हो गए, और वे इसे समझा नहीं पाए।

1650 के दशक में नीदरलैंड्स के वैज्ञानिक क्रिस्टियान हाइगेन्स ने बेहतर दूरबीन से इसका जवाब निकाला। शनि के चारों ओर एक पतला, चपटा छल्ला है, जो ग्रह को छूता नहीं।

ग़ायब होने का यह खेल इसलिए होता है क्योंकि धरती से कभी-कभी छल्ले ठीक किनारे की सीध से दिखते हैं। वे इतने पतले हैं कि लगभग ओझल हो जाते हैं। ऐसा लगभग हर 13 से 16 साल में होता है, और पिछली बार 2025 में हुआ।

सबसे अच्छे नज़दीकी नज़ारे कैसिनी से मिले। इस अंतरिक्ष यान को नासा, यूरोपीय अंतरिक्ष एजेंसी और इटली की अंतरिक्ष एजेंसी ने मिलकर बनाया था। यह 2004 में शनि तक पहुँचा और 13 साल तक उसका अध्ययन करता रहा। इसके कैमरों ने छल्लों में तालाब की लहरियों जैसी लहरें दौड़ती दिखाईं। छोटे चंद्रमा चलते-चलते छल्लों में साफ़ खाली जगहें बुहार देते हैं, और कुछ चंद्रमा भेड़ों को हाँकने वाले कुत्तों की तरह छल्ले के टुकड़ों को पतली धारियों में हाँककर रखते हैं।

2017 में ईंधन ख़त्म होने के क़रीब कैसिनी ने ग्रह और उसके छल्लों के बीच की जगह से 22 साहसी गोते लगाए। फिर वह जानबूझकर शनि में जा समाया। मिशन चलाने वाले पक्का करना चाहते थे कि वह कभी शनि के किसी बर्फ़ीले चंद्रमा से टकराकर वहाँ धरती के कीटाणु न पहुँचा दे।

यहाँ वैज्ञानिकों की राय बँटी हुई है। कैसिनी ने नापा कि अंतरिक्ष से कितनी गहरी धूल लगातार छल्लों पर गिरती रहती है। बर्फ़ अब भी इतनी साफ़ है, इसलिए कुछ शोधकर्ता मानते हैं कि छल्ले नए हैं, शायद कुछ करोड़ साल पुराने। अगर ऐसा है, तो वे शनि के बनने के बहुत बाद बने, शायद तब जब कोई चंद्रमा या [[comet|धूमकेतु]] बहुत पास भटक आया और शनि के [[gravity|गुरुत्वाकर्षण]] ने उसे चीर डाला।

दूसरे वैज्ञानिकों का कहना है कि छल्ले लगभग 4.5 अरब साल पुराने हो सकते हैं, शनि जितने ही, और किसी ऐसे तरीके से साफ़ बने रहे जो हम अभी समझ नहीं पाए।

जो भी हो, छल्ले हमेशा नहीं रहेंगे। अंदरूनी छल्लों की बर्फ़ धीरे-धीरे बरसकर शनि के बादलों में गिरती रहती है। नासा के वैज्ञानिकों की अगुवाई में हुए एक अध्ययन का अनुमान है कि छल्ले लगभग 30 करोड़ साल में ख़त्म हो सकते हैं। डायनासोरों ने कभी बिना छल्लों वाला शनि नहीं देखा, पर हमारी बहुत दूर की पीढ़ियाँ शायद देख लें।

text: Jellyfish sting to catch food and to protect themselves. They have no teeth, claws or bones, and they drift with the currents, so they can't chase prey. Instead, their [[tentacle|tentacles]] are covered in thousands of microscopic stinging cells. When something brushes against them, the cells fire tiny venom-tipped threads into it.

For a small fish or shrimp, the [[venom|venom]] stuns or kills, and the tentacles pull it towards the jellyfish's mouth. For a human, most stings feel like a sharp burning or prickling, with red lines on the skin where the tentacle touched. A few [[species|species]], especially in warm tropical seas, are dangerous.

st.prompt: You've been stung by a jellyfish at the beach and an adult helps you. Which liquid should be used to rinse the sting?
st.reveal: Fresh water can make unfired stinging cells burst and inject more venom, because the change in saltiness triggers them. Sea water rinses the area gently. Urine doesn't help at all. A lifeguard or doctor can advise on what works best for the local jellyfish.

Blow sharply into the other end and watch the paper shoot out and unroll. A real nematocyst works a bit like that, but the thread is far tinier and has a barbed tip.
myth: Peeing on a jellyfish sting makes it better.

sec.t:
The stinging cells are called [[cnidocyte|cnidocytes]]. Inside each one is a tiny capsule holding a long, coiled thread, often with a barbed tip. A trigger on the outside of the cell responds to touch and to chemicals on the skin of prey.

When triggered, pressure inside the capsule shoots the thread out like a harpoon. It turns inside out as it goes, punches through skin and injects venom. The whole thing happens in less than a millionth of a second. Once fired, a cell is used up, and the jellyfish grows a new one.

Jellyfish have been drifting through the oceans for well over 500 million years, long before the first dinosaurs or trees. Their bodies are about 95 per cent water. They have no brain, heart or blood, only a loose net of [[@nervous-system|nerves]] that lets them sense touch, light and which way is up.

They don't decide to sting you. Their cells react automatically to touch. That's why a dead jellyfish on a beach, or a broken bit of tentacle tangled in seaweed, can still sting. It is a good reason never to pick them up. Sometimes jellyfish gather in huge swarms called blooms, which can clog fishing nets and even block the cooling-water pipes of coastal power stations.

sec.h: What to do if you're stung
sec.t:
If you are stung, get out of the water calmly and tell an adult or lifeguard. The adult can rinse the area with sea water and lift off any tentacles using tweezers or a gloved hand. Don't rub it with sand or a towel, because that can make more stinging cells fire.

Soaking the area in water as hot as is comfortable, though never scalding, eases the [[@pain|pain]] for many people. On some Australian beaches, vinegar is kept to treat box jellyfish stings. Anyone who has trouble breathing, feels faint or has a large sting should get medical help immediately. Basic [[@first-aid|first aid]] training covers all of this.

Some animals eat jellyfish without trouble. The leatherback, the largest of the [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]], eats almost nothing else. Its mouth and throat are lined with backward-pointing spines that let it swallow slippery jellies. Sadly, leatherbacks sometimes mistake floating plastic bags for jellyfish.

A tiny blue sea slug, the blue dragon, even eats the Portuguese man o' war and keeps its stinging cells for its own defence.

text: Most door locks are pin tumbler locks. Inside, there is a metal cylinder called the plug, which has to turn for the door to open. Running down into it are five or six tiny pin pairs, each pushed down by a spring. Each pair is split into two pieces, a lower pin and an upper pin, and the pins are all different lengths.

When no key is in the lock, the upper pins poke down into the plug and jam it. Slide in the right key, and its hills and valleys lift each pin pair by just the right amount. Now every split lines up with the edge of the plug, a line called the shear line. Nothing crosses it, so the plug turns and the bolt slides back. The wrong key leaves at least one pin sticking across, and the plug stays stuck.

A tiny camera that checks the key's shape

st.reveal: Each pin is split into two pieces. If a key lifts a pin too little or too much, one piece blocks the line where the plug meets the case, and the plug can't turn. Only when every split lines up exactly does the plug spin free.

myth: Every key in the world is completely unique.

A typical lock has about five or six pins, each cut to one of a handful of depths. That gives tens of thousands of patterns at most, and fewer that work well in practice. With millions of locks around, many share the same pattern. They stay safe mostly because nobody knows which doors match.

sec.h: Wooden keys of the ancient world
sec.t:
The pin idea is very old. About 4,000 years ago, people in [[@ancient-egypt|ancient Egypt]] and Mesopotamia used large wooden locks. A wooden bar held the door shut, and loose wooden pins dropped into holes in the bar to hold it in place. The key was a wooden stick with pegs on it. Pushed in and lifted, its pegs raised the pins and the bar could slide.

Some of these keys were as long as an adult's arm and were carried over the shoulder. The Romans later made smaller metal locks and keys, and some Romans wore little keys as rings on their fingers.

In the 1840s, the American locksmith Linus Yale Sr. built a lock using pins. His son, Linus Yale Jr., shrank the idea into a small cylinder and patented it in the 1860s. He also designed the flat key with a wavy edge that almost everyone still carries.

The design was cheap to make and hard to open without the key. It spread around the world, and the Yale name still appears on many locks today. Most keys in your home, your school and your local bank work the same way.

A combination lock has spinning discs instead of pins. Each disc has a notch, and the right numbers line up all the notches so a bar can drop through. Hotel key cards carry a code on a magnetic strip or a tiny chip. A reader in the door checks the code and releases the bolt with a small motor.

Phones go further still. They read your [[@fingerprints|fingerprint]] or the shape of your face and compare it with a pattern stored inside. In a way, a [[@passwords|password]] is a key too. It is a pattern only you are meant to know, and it only works when every character is in the right place.

असली फ़्रेस्को में रंग गीले पलस्तर पर लगाया जाता है और उसमें सोख लिया जाता है। अजंता में चित्रकार पलस्तर सूखने का इंतज़ार करते थे और रंग टिकाने के लिए गोंद इस्तेमाल करते थे। इसीलिए कुछ रंग पपड़ी बनकर झड़ गया है।

sec.t:
रंग लगाने से पहले खुरदरी चट्टान पर एक चिकनी परत चाहिए थी। मज़दूर चट्टान पर कीचड़ की एक परत दबाकर लगाते थे, जिसमें पत्थर का चूरा, पौधों के रेशे और धान की भूसी मिली होती थी। ये उसे वैसे ही जोड़े रखते थे जैसे कच्चे घर की दीवारों में भूसा। उसके ऊपर चूने की बहुत पतली परत चढ़ाई जाती थी।

अजंता के चित्रों को अक्सर फ़्रेस्को कहा जाता है, पर सख़्ती से देखें तो वे फ़्रेस्को नहीं हैं। असली [[fresco|फ़्रेस्को]] में रंग गीले पलस्तर पर लगता है और उसमें सोख लिया जाता है। अजंता में चित्रकार पलस्तर सूखने का इंतज़ार करते थे और रंग को अपनी जगह टिकाने के लिए गोंद का इस्तेमाल करते थे। यही एक वजह है कि सदियों में कुछ रंग पपड़ी बनकर झड़ गया है, और पीछे भूरी मिट्टी के खाली धब्बे रह गए हैं।

गुफ़ाओं का मुँह नदी की ओर खुलता है, पर उनके अंदरूनी कक्ष धुंधले हैं। चित्रकार कैसे देख पाते थे कि वे क्या बना रहे हैं, यह आज भी एक पहेली है। कुछ इतिहासकार मानते हैं कि वे धूप को अंदर गहराई तक पहुँचाने के लिए शीशों या चमकाई हुई धातु की चादरों का इस्तेमाल करते थे। दूसरे मानते हैं कि तेल के दीये काफ़ी थे, और यह बात रंग में मौजूद दीये की कालिख से भी मेल खाती है।

आज हमें जो रंग दिखते हैं, वे ठीक वही नहीं हैं जो लगाए गए थे। कुछ रंजक उम्र के साथ गहरे हो गए। [[@behind-art-restoration|बाद के मरम्मत करने वालों]] ने जो वार्निश लगाया, वह पीला पड़ गया, और सैलानियों की मशालों के धुएँ ने कुछ दीवारों पर दाग़ छोड़ दिए। रंगों को ठीक से [[@colour-mix|मिलाना]] और टिकाऊ बनाना एक हुनर था, जो बरसों में सीखा जाता था।

एक हज़ार से भी ज़्यादा सालों तक ये गुफ़ाएँ घने जंगल के पीछे लगभग भुला दी गईं। 1819 में जॉन स्मिथ नाम का एक ब्रिटिश सेना अधिकारी बाघ का शिकार कर रहा था, तभी उसे खाई के उस पार एक गुफ़ा का मुँह दिखा। उसने गुफ़ा 10 के एक चित्र पर अपना नाम और तारीख़ खुरच दी, और वह खरोंच आज भी वहीं है।

जल्दी ही कलाकार इन भित्तिचित्रों की नकल बनाने आने लगे। 1900 के दशक की शुरुआत में एक टीम ने, जिसमें युवा भारतीय चित्रकार [[@nandalal-bose|नंदलाल बोस]] भी थे, महीनों तक इनकी नकल बनाई। बरसों बाद बोस और उनके छात्रों ने हाथ से लिखे गए [[@constitution|भारत के संविधान]] की मूल प्रति को सजाया। आज वैज्ञानिक [[@art-detective|कला के जासूसों]] के तरीकों से अजंता के रंग के नन्हे टुकड़ों का अध्ययन करते हैं, ताकि जो बचा है उसे बचाया जा सके।

प्रस्तुति में शुद्ध नृत्य भी होता है, [[rhythm|लय]] और पैरों के काम से भरा, और चेहरे व हाथ के इशारों से भाव भरी कथा भी। बहुत-सी कहानियाँ कृष्ण और राधा के प्रेम की होती हैं। नर्तकी रेशमी साड़ी, चाँदी के गहने और मंदिर के शिखर जैसा मुकुट पहनती है। ओडिसी की जड़ें मंदिर के [[ritual|अनुष्ठानों]] में गहरी धँसी हैं।

sec.t:
सदियों तक ओडिशा में नृत्य मंदिर की पूजा का हिस्सा था। *महारी* कहलाने वाली स्त्रियाँ पुरी के विशाल मंदिर में भगवान जगन्नाथ के लिए नाचती थीं। समय के साथ *गोटीपुआ* कहलाने वाले लड़के भी लड़कियों के वेश में गाँव के उत्सवों में नाचने लगे। उनकी शैली में करतब ज़्यादा थे, शरीर को मोड़ना और संतुलन साधना।

1900 की शुरुआत तक दोनों परंपराएँ फीकी पड़ रही थीं। महारी प्रथा का सहारा छिन चुका था, और ओडिशा से बाहर बहुत कम लोगों ने यह नृत्य कभी देखा था।

1940 के दशक के आखिर और 1950 के दशक में गुरुओं, विद्वानों और नर्तकों का एक समूह इस कला को फिर से जीवित करने निकला। बचपन में गोटीपुआ के रूप में नाच चुके केलुचरण महापात्र इन गुरुओं में सबसे मशहूर हुए। दूसरों में पंकज चरण दास और देबप्रसाद दास थे।

उन्होंने समझा कि महारियों और गोटीपुओं को क्या याद था, मुद्राओं का मिलान मंदिर की मूर्तियों से किया, और नृत्य पर पुराने ग्रंथ पढ़े। इन सबसे उन्होंने प्रस्तुतियों का एक साफ़ ढाँचा खड़ा किया। संजुक्ता पाणिग्रही जैसी शिष्याएँ ओडिसी को पूरे भारत और विदेशों के मंचों तक ले गईं। आज यह भुवनेश्वर से लेकर न्यू जर्सी और कैलिफ़ोर्निया तक के नृत्य विद्यालयों में सिखाया जाता है।

sec.h: शुरू से आखिर तक एक प्रस्तुति
sec.t:
ओडिसी की प्रस्तुति अक्सर *मंगलाचरण* से शुरू होती है, जो देवताओं और धरती को अर्पण है। इसके बाद शुद्ध नृत्य का एक टुकड़ा आता है, जो ताल और चाल के पैटर्न रचता है। फिर भाव वाले टुकड़े आते हैं, जिनमें नर्तक चेहरे, आँखों और हाथों से किसी गीत का अभिनय करता है।

इनमें से बहुत-से गीत *गीत गोविंद* से आते हैं, जो राधा और कृष्ण पर संस्कृत की एक [[@poetry|कविता]] है और जिसे 12वीं सदी में पुरी से जुड़े कवि जयदेव ने लिखा। प्रस्तुति अक्सर *मोक्ष* पर खत्म होती है, जिसका मतलब है मुक्ति। यह एक तेज़, आनंद भरा नृत्य है जो पूरी तरह थम जाने पर खत्म होता है।

ओडिसी नर्तक ओडिशा के [[loom|करघों]] पर हाथ से बुनी रेशमी साड़ियाँ पहनते हैं, अक्सर ऐसी चुन्नटों में बाँधकर जो घुटने मुड़ते ही पंखे की तरह खुल जाती हैं। चाँदी के गहने आम तौर पर कटक की तारकशी के होते हैं, जो बारीक ऐंठे तारों से बनते हैं। लाल आलता हाथों और पैरों को रँगता है, ताकि हर इशारा उभरकर दिखे। मुकुट, जिसे टाहिया कहते हैं, हल्की सफ़ेद सोला (शोला) से बनता है और मंदिर के शिखर जैसा होता है।

संगीत मर्दल पर बजता है, जो पीपे जैसा ढोल है, साथ में एक गायक, बाँसुरी, वायलिन या सितार और छोटी झाँझें। ओडिशा के चित्रित पट, जिन्हें [[@pattachitra|पट्टचित्र]] कहते हैं, कृष्ण और राधा की वही कहानियाँ दिखाते हैं जिन्हें नर्तक मंच पर निभाते हैं।

text: A budget is a plan for money. It has three parts: how much comes in, how much goes out and how much is left over.

To make one, first write down all your income, such as pocket money, gifts or money for jobs. Then list what you spend or need to spend. Take the second number away from the first. If there is money left, you can save it or plan something with it. If you are spending more than you get, something has to change.
Families, shops, schools, companies and whole countries all make budgets. The numbers get bigger, but the idea stays the same.

st.reveal: The rule suggests 50% for needs, 30% for wants and 20% for savings. Twenty per cent of ₹500 is ₹100. It's a rough guide, not a law, and many families adjust it to fit their lives.

sec.t:
The first step in budgeting is sorting your spending. **Needs** are things you must have, like food, rent, school fees and bus fares. **Wants** are things that are nice to have, like a new video game, cinema tickets or a fancy pencil case.

A popular rule of thumb is the 50/30/20 rule. It was made popular by the American writers Elizabeth Warren and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi in a 2005 book. It suggests spending about 50% of your income on needs, 30% on wants and 20% on savings. Real families change these numbers to suit their lives, but it is a handy starting point.

Every year, the Government of India presents a Union Budget to [[@parliament-india|Parliament]]. It shows how much money the government expects to collect, mostly from [[@taxes|taxes]]. It also shows how it plans to spend it on things like defence, roads, railways, schools, hospitals and paying interest on its loans.

The first budget in British India was presented on 7 April 1860 by James Wilson, a Scottish economist who had earlier founded *The Economist* magazine. After Independence, India's first finance minister, R.K. Shanmukham Chetty, presented a budget on 26 November 1947. Since 2017, the Union Budget has been presented on 1 February each year.

The United States government plans its spending in a similar way. Its year for budgeting, called the fiscal year, starts on 1 October.

If a government spends more than it collects, the gap is called a deficit. It borrows money to fill the gap and pays interest on the loan. If it collects more than it spends, that is a surplus.

Households work the same way. Borrowing can make sense for something large, like a house or a college course. But borrowing to pay for everyday wants can lead to debts that grow faster than savings ever could.

A budget tells you what a family or a country cares about. A family saving for a trip might cut down on eating out. A country that spends more on schools one year is making a choice.

[[@newspapers|Newspapers]] often show the government's budget as a [[@graphs-charts|pie chart]], with a slice for each kind of spending. Looking at the slices is one of the quickest ways to see where the money goes.

text: Surfers ride waves by sliding down the steep front of a wave as it moves towards the shore. A surfer lies on the board and paddles hard to match the wave's speed. As the wave lifts the back of the board, [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] pulls the surfer down its slope. The surfer pops up to standing and steers along the wave's face, staying just ahead of the part that is breaking.

It works a bit like sledding down a hill that keeps moving forward and building itself again in front of you. Surfing began among Polynesian peoples, especially in Hawaii, centuries ago. Today it is an Olympic sport, and there are surfers on beaches from California to Kerala.

st.prompt: Why do surfers paddle hard just before a wave reaches them?

options.t: To match the wave's speed so it can carry them
To keep warm in cold water

st.reveal: A wave moves fast. If a surfer is still, it just lifts them and passes underneath. By paddling hard, they get moving fast enough that the steep front of the wave catches the board, and gravity pulls them down its face.

In open water, a wave is energy moving through the sea, and the water itself mostly goes round in circles. Surfers ride the moving slope of the wave as it breaks, sliding down it while it travels forward.
facts: wind blowing over the ocean, often from distant storms

sec.t:
Most surfing [[@waves-how|waves]] are made by wind. When wind blows over the sea for a long time and a long distance, it builds ripples into rolling waves called swell. Storms can send swell thousands of kilometres across the ocean. A wave that breaks on a beach in Hawaii may have started in a storm near Antarctica days earlier.

In deep water, a wave is mostly energy passing through. As it reaches shallower water near the shore, its bottom drags on the seabed and slows. The top keeps going, the wave gets steeper and taller, and finally it tips over and breaks.

sec.h: Sliding on waves in old Hawaii
sec.t:
[[@polynesians|Polynesian]] peoples were surfing long before Europeans arrived. In Hawaii it was called he'e nalu, wave sliding. Chiefs rode long, heavy boards made of wood, some more than 4 metres long. Ordinary people rode shorter boards. Surfing contests were part of festivals.

In 1778 and 1779, officers on Captain James Cook's voyage described Hawaiians riding waves and were amazed. In the early 1900s, the Hawaiian swimmer Duke Kahanamoku, an Olympic champion, showed off surfing in Australia and California and helped spread it worldwide. Bored surfers in California later put wheels on boards, and [[@skateboarding|skateboarding]] was born.

At Nazaré, on Portugal's coast, a deep underwater canyon funnels ocean swell straight at the shore, making some of the biggest waves anyone surfs. In October 2020, the German surfer Sebastian Steudtner rode one measured at 26.21 metres. Guinness World Records lists it as the largest wave ever surfed. That same year, Brazil's Maya Gabeira set the women's record there, at about 22.4 metres.

Waves that big move too fast to paddle into. So surfers are towed in by a partner on a jet ski.

sec.h: Surfing at the Olympics and in India
sec.t:
Surfing first appeared at the [[@olympics|Olympics]] at Tokyo 2020, held in 2021 because of the [[pandemic|pandemic]]. For Paris 2024, the surfing was held at Teahupo'o in Tahiti, a French [[territory|territory]] in the Pacific, famous for its thick, heavy waves breaking over a shallow reef.

In India, surfing grew from the 2000s, with surf schools along the coasts of Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu. And the strangest part? The fastest, most powerful waves of all, [[@tsunami|tsunamis]], are almost impossible to surf. In deep water they are barely a ripple, and near land they arrive as a rising flood.

text: Stories that last often have clever heroes, tricky problems and a lesson tucked inside.
They change as they travel. Each storyteller adds a little, so one tale can have hundreds of versions.

Telling stories might be one of the oldest things humans do, maybe as old as language itself. Long before writing, people remembered stories by telling them again and again. The ones that were easy to remember, useful to know and fun to hear were the ones that survived.

sec.t:
The Panchatantra is a collection of animal fables from ancient India. Tradition says a wise teacher named Vishnu Sharma told them to three lazy princes, to teach them how to live wisely. The stories sit inside one another, like boxes within boxes. A character starts telling a tale, and inside that tale another character tells another.

In one famous story, a crocodile befriends a monkey who gives him sweet fruit. The crocodile's wife wants to eat the monkey's heart, so the crocodile carries the monkey across the river on his back. Halfway, he admits the plan. The quick-thinking monkey says he left his heart in the tree, and must go back to fetch it. He escapes, and the friendship ends.

India's great epics, the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and the Mahabharata, were sung and told aloud for generations before being written down. The Vedas were memorised so carefully, with special chanting patterns, that they were passed on almost word for word for thousands of years. UNESCO recognises this Vedic chanting as part of the world's cultural heritage.

Repetition, [[rhythm|rhythm]] and patterns helped. Many stories use things in threes, like three wishes or three brothers. Animals stand for human types: the clever fox, the boastful lion, the [[@crow-smart|crafty crow]]. These patterns make stories easier to remember and retell.

sec.h: How old can a story be?
sec.t:
The Epic of Gilgamesh, from [[@mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], was written on clay tablets about 4,000 years ago. But some stories may be older than [[@writing-began|writing]] itself. In 2016, two researchers compared [[@indian-folk-tales|folk tales]] across many languages, using methods [[biologist|biologists]] use to build family trees. They suggested that a tale called "The Smith and the Devil" might be around 6,000 years old. Not everyone agrees, but it is a clever way to look into the past.

Cinderella-style stories turn up all over the world too. A Greek writer told one about a girl named Rhodopis over 2,000 years ago, and a Chinese version, about a girl named Ye Xian, was written down in the 800s CE.

Old stories keep finding new homes. In 1967, Anant Pai started [[@amar-chitra-katha|Amar Chitra Katha]] to tell Indian history and legends as comics. In 1986, [[@rk-narayan|R.K. Narayan]]'s stories about Malgudi, a small South Indian town, became a much-loved TV show. Today, films, games and apps retell the same tales, and a child in Chennai and a child in Chicago may both know the monkey who left his heart in the tree.

text: Women's cricket is very old but has grown fastest in the last ten years. Women played in English villages in the 1700s, and the first Women's World Cup took place in 1973. For decades, though, players paid their own way, played in front of tiny crowds and were barely shown on television.

Since about 2017, that has changed sharply. Big audiences, professional leagues, better pay and television deals have turned women's cricket into a major sport, especially in India, Australia and England.

sec.t:
The first recorded women's match took place in Surrey, England, in 1745, between two villages. [[@newspapers|Newspapers]] reported that the women "bowled, batted, ran and catched" as well as most men.

There is a popular story that round-arm bowling was invented by a woman, Christina Willes, in the early 1800s, because her wide skirt got in the way of underarm bowling. Historians say it is a nice tale but hard to prove.

The Women's Cricket Association of India was set up in 1973, and India's women played their first Test in 1976, against the West Indies in [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]]. Shantha Rangaswamy captained that first Test side. For years players travelled in unreserved train compartments and stayed in cheap lodgings. Things improved after 2006, when the women's association merged into the BCCI, which ran men's cricket and had far more money.

Two players defined the next era. [[@mithali-raj|Mithali Raj]], a batter from Hyderabad, played international cricket for 23 years and scored more one-day runs than any other woman. Fast bowler Jhulan Goswami, from a small town in West Bengal, took more one-day wickets than anyone else when she retired in 2022.

India's women reached the 2017 World Cup final in England. In the semi-final, Harmanpreet Kaur hit 171 not out against Australia. India then lost the final at Lord's in [[@london|London]] to England by just nine runs.

Millions watched in India, many of them seeing women's cricket for the first time. Sponsors, broadcasters and the BCCI took notice.

In 2022 the BCCI announced that India's women would earn the same match fees as men. Their yearly contracts are still smaller. In 2023 the Women's Premier League began, an [[@ipl|IPL]]-style league with city teams and a player auction. Mumbai Indians won its first season, and several players earned more in one auction than in years of playing before.

In November 2025, India's women won their first 50-over World Cup, beating South Africa in the final at Navi Mumbai. Captain Harmanpreet Kaur's team joined the men's heroes in India's [[@cricket-world-cups|World Cup]] story. Girls' cricket academies across India report more players than ever, and the women's game now writes fresh chapters of [[@cricket-history|cricket history]] every season.

text: Galileo Galilei was an Italian scientist who lived about 400 years ago. He was one of the first people to study the sky with a telescope. He found mountains on the Moon, four moons orbiting [[@jupiter-giant|Jupiter]], countless stars in the [[@milky-way|Milky Way]] and [[@sunspots|spots on the Sun]].

He also did careful experiments with rolling balls and swinging weights, and showed that maths could describe how things move. His support for the idea that the Earth goes round the Sun brought him into conflict with the Catholic Church, and he spent his last years under house arrest.

sec.t:
Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564. His father, a musician, wanted him to become a doctor, but Galileo preferred mathematics. An old story says that as a student he watched a lamp swinging in Pisa Cathedral and timed it with his pulse. He noticed that big swings and small swings took about the same time. The story may be polished in the retelling, but he did study [[pendulum|pendulums]], and his idea was later used to make accurate [[@clocks|clocks]].

Another famous story says he dropped two balls of different weights from the Leaning Tower of Pisa to show they land together. He may never have done this exactly. He did show, by rolling balls down slopes, that heavy and light objects speed up at the same rate if air does not slow them down.

sec.h: A new window on the sky

sec.t:
At the time, most people, including Church leaders, believed the Earth sat still at the centre of the universe. The Polish [[astronomer|astronomer]] Copernicus had suggested in 1543 that the Earth moves round the Sun. Galileo's discoveries convinced him Copernicus was right.

In 1616, Church authorities told him not to teach the idea as fact. In 1632 he published a book that argued for it anyway. The next year he was put on trial by the Roman Inquisition, a Church court. He was made to say publicly that he rejected the idea. He spent the rest of his life under house arrest at his villa in Arcetri, near Florence, where he kept working and writing, even after he went blind.

A legend says that after the trial he muttered "And yet it moves", meaning the Earth. There is no record of this from the time.

Galileo's habit of testing ideas with experiments and measurements is one reason he is often called a father of modern science. He lived during the late [[@renaissance|Renaissance]], when Italian thinkers and artists were questioning old ideas.

In 1992, Pope John Paul II formally accepted that the Church had been wrong to condemn him. NASA named a spacecraft after him. Launched in 1989, it orbited Jupiter for nearly eight years and studied the four moons Galileo found. They are still called the Galilean moons: Io, [[@europa|Europa]], Ganymede and Callisto. Two of his telescopes survive at the Museo Galileo in Florence.

text: ISRO, the Indian Space Research Organisation, launches most of its rockets from the [[@launch-sites|Satish Dhawan Space Centre]] at Sriharikota. It is an island on the coast of Andhra Pradesh, about 80 km north of Chennai. A rocket is put together in a huge building, rolled to the launch pad, filled with fuel, and launched when a [[@maths-countdown|computer-controlled countdown]] reaches zero.

The rocket burns its fuel in stages. Each stage fires, empties and falls away into the sea, making the rocket lighter. Within about 20 minutes, the final stage releases the satellite into [[orbit|orbit]] around the Earth.

st.reveal: Rockets launched eastwards get a push from Earth's spin, which is fastest near the equator. Open sea to the east means used rocket stages fall safely into the water, far from towns.

sec.h: Why an island in the east?
sec.t:
Sriharikota sits close to the [[equator|equator]], at about 13.7° north. The Earth spins eastwards, and near the equator the ground moves at more than 1,600 km/h. A rocket launched east carries that speed with it, a free head start that saves fuel.

The island also has the Bay of Bengal to its east. Spent stages and any failed rocket fall into empty sea, not on villages. The site was chosen in the late 1960s and first used in 1971.

India's space story began at Thumba, [[@people-fishing-villages|a fishing village]] near Thiruvananthapuram, which sits almost on the magnetic equator, a good place to study the upper [[atmosphere|atmosphere]]. On 21 November 1963, scientists launched a small American-made sounding rocket there. A local church became an office, and rocket parts were famously carried on [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]] and a bullock cart.

The programme was led by [[@vikram-sarabhai|Vikram Sarabhai]]. A young engineer named [[@apj-kalam|A.P.J. Abdul Kalam]] later led the team that built SLV-3. On 18 July 1980 it put the Rohini satellite into orbit, making India one of only a handful of countries able to launch its own satellites.

For days before a launch, teams check every valve, wire and computer. The fuel is loaded, the launch pad is cleared, and engineers in the Mission Control Centre watch hundreds of readings on their screens. In the final minutes, an automatic launch sequence takes over. If any reading looks wrong, the computer can stop the countdown.

After lift-off, ground stations across India and abroad track the rocket. The [[@rockets-how|rocket's]] path is planned in advance, but small engines and steering nozzles keep it on course, adjusting many times a second.

On 15 February 2017, a PSLV carried 104 satellites into orbit in one launch, a world record at the time. Most were small imaging satellites the size of a shoebox, owned by an American company. They were released one after another over about ten minutes, each into a slightly different path so they wouldn't bump into each other.

ISRO has also launched hundreds of satellites for other countries. Its rockets are thrown away after one use, but ISRO is now testing a winged, [[@reusable-rockets|reusable]] vehicle called Pushpak that glides back to land on a runway like a plane.

text: The first people to reach the South Pole were Norwegian explorer Roald Amundsen and four companions, on 14 December 1911. A British team led by Robert Falcon Scott arrived about five weeks later and found the Norwegian flag already there.

The North Pole is trickier. In 1909, American Robert Peary said he had reached it with Matthew Henson and four Inuit men. Another American, Frederick Cook, said he had got there a year earlier. Neither could prove it, and most experts now doubt both. The first undisputed view of the North Pole came from an [[@sky-blimps|airship]] flying over it in 1926.

sec.t:
By 1900, explorers had mapped most coastlines on Earth. The poles, the very top and bottom of the planet, were the last great "firsts". Reaching one meant fame for the explorer and pride for their country.

The two poles are very different. The South Pole sits high on the ice sheet of [[@antarctica|Antarctica]], a frozen continent, about 2,800 m above sea level. The North Pole is out on the sea ice of the [[@arctic|Arctic]] Ocean.

Amundsen had first planned to go north. When he heard Peary and Cook had claimed the North Pole, he secretly turned his ship south instead.

His [[expedition|expedition]] brought nearly 100 sled dogs to Antarctica, and the polar team travelled on skis. They dressed in fur clothing based on what Inuit people wore. They left supplies along the way and marked their route with flags. They reached the Pole after about eight weeks of travel and left a tent with a letter for Scott.

Scott's team used ponies, dogs and motor sledges. The ponies struggled, the motors broke and the men ended up pulling heavy sledges themselves. They reached the Pole on 17 January 1912, exhausted and disappointed. All five died of cold and hunger on the long journey back. Their [[@diaries|diaries]] were found later and made them famous in Britain.

Peary had spent years in the Arctic, relying on Inuit guides and on Matthew Henson, an African American explorer who worked with him for about twenty years. In April 1909 Peary claimed they had reached the Pole.

Cook said he had arrived in April 1908 with two Inuit companions. The two men argued bitterly in [[@newspapers|newspapers]]. Experts later questioned their records. Peary's speeds seemed too fast, and Cook's evidence was thin.

Proving it was hard because the ice drifts, and navigators had to work out position from the Sun with handheld instruments. Near the poles the Sun stays low, and in the Arctic spring it never sets, so the [[@north-star|North Star]] could not help either.

{{story:earth-magnet}}

The airship *Norge*, carrying Amundsen, American Lincoln Ellsworth and Italian Umberto Nobile, flew over the North Pole in May 1926. That made Amundsen and his teammate Oscar Wisting, who had also stood at the South Pole, the first people accepted as having seen both poles.

India sent its first expedition to Antarctica in 1981–82. In 1983 it set up its first research station, Dakshin Gangotri. Today it runs two stations there, [[@antarctica-stations|Maitri and Bharati]], where scientists study ice, weather and [[climate|climate]].

In the Arctic, India opened a research station called Himadri in Norway's [[@world-svalbard|Svalbard]] islands in 2008.

The USA has run a research station exactly at the South Pole since 1956, named after Amundsen and Scott. In summer, more than a hundred people live there. Scientists study the stars, the ice and Earth's changing climate, in the place two teams once struggled for weeks just to reach.

text: [[hieroglyphs|चित्रलिपि]] प्राचीन मिस्र की चित्रों जैसी लिपि थी, जो 3,000 से ज़्यादा साल तक इस्तेमाल हुई। जब मिस्र रोमन शासन में आया और बाद में ईसाई बना, तो इसे सीखने वाले घटते गए। लगभग 400 ईसवी तक कोई इन्हें नहीं पढ़ पाता था, और लगभग 1,400 साल तक इनका मतलब खोया रहा।

इन्हें फिर से पढ़ने की चाबी बना रोज़ेटा पत्थर। उस पर एक ही संदेश तीन बार लिखा है: चित्रलिपि में, डेमोटिक नाम की रोज़मर्रा की मिस्री लिपि में, और प्राचीन यूनानी में, जिसे विद्वान तब भी पढ़ सकते थे। तीनों को मिलाकर, और मिस्री भाषा के बाद के रूप कॉप्टिक की जानकारी के सहारे, फ़्रांसीसी विद्वान ज़ाँ-फ़्रांस्वा शांपोलियों ने 1822 में यह गुत्थी सुलझा ली।

sec.t:
जुलाई 1799 में फ़्रांसीसी सैनिक [[@egypt-nile|नील]] के [[delta|डेल्टा]] में रशीद शहर के पास एक पुराना क़िला दोबारा बना रहे थे। यूरोप के लोग इस शहर को रोज़ेटा कहते थे। [[@napoleon|नेपोलियन]] ने एक साल पहले मिस्र पर हमला किया था। पत्थरों के बीच एक अफ़सर की नज़र लिखावट से भरी एक गहरे रंग की शिला पर पड़ी।

यह पत्थर लगभग 760 किलो का है, यानी लगभग चार भारी मोटरसाइकिलों जितना, और इसका एक हिस्सा टूटा हुआ है। जब अंग्रेज़ों ने मिस्र में फ़्रांसीसियों को हराया, तो पत्थर उन्हें सौंप दिया गया। 1802 से यह ब्रिटिश म्यूज़ियम में है, और आज वहाँ सबसे ज़्यादा देखी जाने वाली चीज़ों में से एक है। मिस्र इसे वापस माँग चुका है।

अंग्रेज़ वैज्ञानिक थॉमस यंग ने एक अहम शुरुआत की। उन्होंने देखा कि कुछ चित्र-चिह्न अंडाकार घेरों में बंद हैं, जिन्हें आज कार्टूश कहते हैं। उन्होंने अंदाज़ा लगाया कि इनमें राजाओं के नाम हैं, और पता लगाया कि एक घेरे में टॉलेमी लिखा है।

शांपोलियों इससे बहुत आगे गए। उन्होंने रोज़ेटा पत्थर के कार्टूश को एक दूसरे कार्टूश से मिलाया, जिसमें क्लियोपेट्रा का नाम था। दोनों में साझा ध्वनियाँ, जैसे प, त, ओ और ल, एक ही चिह्नों से लिखी थीं। फिर उन्होंने सूरज के लिए कॉप्टिक शब्द *रा* की मदद से एक मंदिर की नक्काशी पर फ़राओ रामसेस का नाम पढ़ लिया। इससे साबित हुआ कि मिस्री नामों के लिए भी ध्वनि-चिह्न इस्तेमाल होते थे, और पूरी पद्धति खुलने लगी। परिवार में एक किस्सा चलता है कि जब उन्हें यह समझ आया, तो वे दौड़कर अपने भाई के दफ़्तर पहुँचे, चिल्लाए "मिल गया!" और बेहोश हो गए।

चित्रलिपि में तीन तरह के चिह्न मिले-जुले हैं। कुछ एक-एक ध्वनि दिखाते हैं, जैसे किसी [[@alphabet-history|वर्णमाला]] के अक्षर। कुछ दो या तीन ध्वनियाँ एक साथ। और कुछ ऐसे चित्र हैं जो मतलब बताते हैं, जैसे किसी इंसान वाले शब्द के बाद बैठे हुए आदमी का छोटा-सा चित्र। लिखने वाले स्वर नहीं लिखते थे, इसलिए हमें पक्का नहीं पता कि बहुत से शब्द बोले कैसे जाते थे।

नियमित इस्तेमाल में सैकड़ों चिह्न थे। इन्हें अच्छी तरह लिखने में बरसों का अभ्यास लगता था, इसलिए मिस्री लोग रोज़ के कामकाज के लिए तेज़, जुड़ी हुई लिपियाँ भी इस्तेमाल करते थे।

sec.h: लिपियाँ जो अब भी पढ़ी जा रही हैं
sec.t:
पुरानी लिपियों को पढ़ने का काम आज भी जारी है। भारत में [[@ashoka|अशोक]] के [[inscription|शिलालेखों]] वाली ब्राह्मी लिपि सदियों से भुला दी गई थी। कलकत्ता के एक अफ़सर जेम्स प्रिंसेप ने 1837 में साँची के छोटे, बार-बार दोहराए गए दान-लेखों को आपस में मिलाकर इसे पढ़ लिया।

कुछ लिपियाँ आज भी अनपढ़ी हैं। [[@indus-cities|सिंधु के शहरों]] की मुहरों पर बने चिह्न अब तक हर कोशिश को मात देते आए हैं। लेख छोटे हैं, और साथ में अनुवाद वाला कोई रोज़ेटा पत्थर नहीं है। शायद किसी खेत में या किसी संग्रहालय की दराज़ में वह चाबी इंतज़ार कर रही हो।

text: नाचने की महामारी 1518 में स्ट्रासबर्ग शहर में फैली एक अजीब घटना थी। यह जुलाई में शुरू हुई, जब एक औरत, जिसे बाद की कहानियों में फ़्राउ ट्रॉफ़िया कहा गया, सड़क पर नाचने लगी और कई दिन नाचती रही। जल्द ही दूसरे लोग भी उसके साथ जुड़ गए। कुछ हफ़्तों में दर्जनों लोग नाच रहे थे, कुछ तो लगातार कई-कई दिन। उनके चेहरों पर खुशी कम, परेशानी ज़्यादा दिखती थी।

शहर के दस्तावेज़ों और इतिहास-ग्रंथों में इसका ज़िक्र है, इसलिए यह सचमुच हुआ था। पर ऐसा क्यों हुआ, यह उतना साफ़ नहीं। आज ज़्यादातर इतिहासकार मानते हैं कि यह किसी कीटाणु या ज़हर से नहीं, बल्कि सामूहिक मनोवैज्ञानिक बीमारी से हुआ। यह एक तरह की घबराहट है जो डरे हुए समाज में एक से दूसरे तक फैल जाती है।

sec.t:
1518 का स्ट्रासबर्ग रहने के लिए कठिन जगह था। लगातार कई साल फ़सलें खराब हुई थीं और लोग भूखे थे। चेचक जैसी बीमारियाँ और सिफ़लिस नाम की एक नई बीमारी फैल रही थी। बहुत-से परिवार गरीब थे और कर्ज़ में डूबे थे।

लोग यह भी मानते थे कि संत पापियों को बीमारी देकर सज़ा दे सकते हैं। कहा जाता था कि संत वाइटस किसी को ऐसा श्राप दे सकते हैं कि वह नाचे बिना रह ही न पाए। ऐसे माहौल में डर और थकान एक आदमी से दूसरे तक बहुत तेज़ी से फैल सकते थे।

स्ट्रासबर्ग की घटना पहली नहीं थी। 1374 में नाचने वालों की टोलियाँ राइन नदी के किनारे के कस्बों से गुज़रीं, जिनमें आखन और कोलोन भी थे। उन पर भी ऐसा ही जुनून सवार था। यूरोप के दूसरे हिस्सों में भी लगभग 300 साल तक छोटी-छोटी ऐसी घटनाएँ होती रहीं, अक्सर [[famine|अकाल]] या बीमारी के दिनों में, जैसे [[@black-death|ब्लैक डेथ]] के बाद के सालों में।

बाद में डॉक्टरी भाषा में "संत वाइटस का नाच" नाम इसी इतिहास से आया। आज डॉक्टर उन अलग-अलग बीमारियों के लिए दूसरे नाम इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जिन्हें कभी यह नाम दिया जाता था।

एक पुराना अनुमान अर्गट को दोषी मानता था। यह एक [[fungus|फफूँद]] है, जो नमी वाली राई पर उगती है। संक्रमित राई की रोटी खाने से भ्रम हो सकते हैं और शरीर फड़क सकता है। पर अर्गट हाथ-पैरों में खून का बहाव भी रोक देता है, जिससे घंटों नाचना मुश्किल है, कई दिन की तो बात ही छोड़ो। इसलिए ज़्यादातर इतिहासकार अब इस पर शक करते हैं। कुछ फफूँद दिमाग पर असर डालती ज़रूर हैं, जैसा [[@mushrooms|कुकुरमुत्तों]] की कहानी से पता चलता है, पर अर्गट तथ्यों पर ठीक नहीं बैठता।

इतिहासकार जॉन वॉलर का कहना है कि यह सामूहिक मनोवैज्ञानिक बीमारी थी। भूखे, डरे हुए और यह माने बैठे लोग कि उन पर श्राप है, एक तरह की बेसुध हालत में चले गए। दूसरों को नाचते देखकर और लोगों को भी लगने लगा कि उन पर भी श्राप है। डॉक्टर जानते हैं कि [[@stress|तनाव]] और डर से शरीर में सचमुच के [[symptom|लक्षण]] पैदा हो सकते हैं।

ऐसी घटनाएँ आज भी होती हैं। 1962 में टांगानिका, जो अब तंज़ानिया है, के लड़कियों के एक बोर्डिंग स्कूल से बेकाबू हँसी आसपास के गाँवों तक फैल गई। कई स्कूल कुछ समय के लिए बंद करने पड़े। 2001 में दिल्ली के कई इलाकों में अफ़वाह फैली कि रात में कोई "मंकी मैन" लोगों पर हमला करता है। खूब दहशत फैली, पर ऐसा कोई जीव कभी नहीं मिला।

ये घटनाएँ दिखाती हैं कि मन कितना ताकतवर है और भावनाएँ भीड़ में कैसे दौड़ती हैं। इसका एक हल्का-फुल्का रूप तुम रोज़ देखते हो: कमरे में एक को उबासी आई और देखते-देखते सबको आने लगी, या क्लास में किसी एक की [[@laughter|हँसी]] छूटी और पूरी क्लास हँसने लगी।

text: The Rajputs are a group of clans, or extended families, from north and central India, especially Rajasthan. The word comes from the Sanskrit *rajaputra*, "son of a king". From about the 7th and 8th centuries, Rajput families ruled kingdoms across the region, including Mewar, Marwar, Amber and Ajmer.

They became famous as warriors and fort-builders. Over the centuries, Rajput kingdoms fought the Delhi Sultans, the [[@mughals|Mughals]] and each other. Many made alliances with the Mughals and served as their generals. Rajput rulers survived into British times as princes, and their forts and palaces still dominate the skyline of Rajasthan.

myth: The Rajputs were always united against outside rulers.

Rajput clans often fought each other, and many made alliances with the Delhi Sultans and later the Mughals. Some, like Mewar, resisted for a long time, while others, like Amber, became close Mughal allies.

sec.t:
Historians disagree about Rajput origins. A [[medieval|medieval]] legend says the four great clans were born from a sacred fire on Mount Abu. In the 1800s, some British writers argued that the Rajputs were descended from Central Asian invaders. Many modern historians think the clans formed from local landholding and warrior families who gained power and claimed ancient royal ancestors.

What is clear is that, by around 1000 CE, families like the Chauhans of Ajmer, the Gahadavalas of Kannauj and the Guhilas of Mewar were ruling kingdoms and building forts and temples.

The most famous early Rajput king is Prithviraj Chauhan, who ruled from Ajmer and Delhi. In 1191 he defeated the invading ruler Muhammad Ghori at the first battle of Tarain, near today's Karnal in Haryana.

Ghori returned the next year, in 1192, and won. Prithviraj was captured and killed. Ghori's general later became the first sultan of Delhi, and the [[@delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] began. Prithviraj's life was retold in a long Hindi poem, the *Prithviraj Raso*, which mixes history with legend.

sec.h: Friends and enemies of the Mughals
sec.t:
When the Mughals arrived, the Rajputs had to choose. Rana Sanga of Mewar led a big alliance against the first Mughal emperor, Babur, but lost at Khanwa in 1527.

[[@akbar|Akbar]] took a different path. He married Rajput princesses, gave Rajput kings high ranks and let them keep their lands. Raja Man Singh of Amber became one of his top generals. Mewar held out. In 1576 Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's army, led by Man Singh, at Haldighati. The battle was indecisive, but Pratap kept resisting from the hills for the rest of his life, and is remembered as a hero of independence.

Rajput courts were also centres of art. Artists painted bright [[@myths-krishna-childhood|miniatures of Krishna]], court life and the seasons. [[@mirabai-kabir|Mirabai]], a Rajput princess of the 1500s, gave up palace life to sing songs of love for Krishna that are still sung across India.

Under British rule, Rajput kingdoms became princely states such as Udaipur, Jodhpur and Jaipur. After 1947 they joined India. Today six Rajasthan hill forts, including Chittorgarh and Kumbhalgarh, form a single [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]].

text: For more than a thousand years, the region that is now Bihar sat at the centre of Indian history. It was the heart of Magadha, the kingdom that grew into the [[@mauryan-empire|Mauryan Empire]], India's first [[empire|empire]] to cover most of the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]]. Its capital, Pataliputra, is today's Patna.

Bihar is also where two great religious teachers lived and taught. The Buddha attained enlightenment at [[@bodh-gaya|Bodh Gaya]], and Mahavira, the great teacher of Jainism, was born and died in the region. Later came Nalanda, one of the world's great centres of learning. Even the state's name comes from vihara, the word for a Buddhist [[monastery|monastery]].

sec.t:
In the 5th century BCE, or perhaps a little earlier, a prince named Siddhartha Gautama left his comfortable life to search for an answer to human suffering. According to Buddhist tradition, he sat in [[@mindfulness|meditation]] under a pipal tree at Bodh Gaya and reached enlightenment. From then on he was called the [[@buddha|Buddha]], "the awakened one".

A [[descendant|descendant]] of that tree still grows beside the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2002. Buddhists from Sri Lanka, [[@thailand|Thailand]], Japan, Tibet and many other places travel there to pray. Monasteries built by many of those countries now stand around the town, each in its own national style.

At around the same time, [[@mahavira|Mahavira]] taught non-violence towards all living things. Jain tradition says he was born near Vaishali and reached his final liberation at Pavapuri, both in Bihar.

sec.h: A university of the ancient world
sec.t:
From the 5th century CE, Nalanda grew into a vast [[@hist-first-university|monastery-university]]. Students came from China, Korea, Tibet and South-East Asia to study Buddhism, logic, grammar, medicine and [[@astronomy-ancient-india|astronomy]]. The Chinese traveller Xuanzang studied there in the 7th century and wrote about its towers, libraries and strict entrance tests.

Nalanda was attacked and badly damaged around the end of the 12th century, and slowly fell into ruin. Its red-brick remains were excavated much later and became a World Heritage Site in 2016. The great mathematician [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]], born in 476 CE, is also linked to the region, and is often said to have worked near Pataliputra.

sec.h: A republic, a Guru and a satyagraha
sec.t:
Vaishali was home to the Licchavis, who were governed by an assembly of leading families rather than a single king. That's why it is often called one of the world's earliest [[republic|republics]], although historians debate how far it was like a modern republic.

Bihar's story kept going. Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, was born in Patna in 1666, and a gurdwara marks the place. In 1917, [[@gandhi-south-africa|Gandhi]] led his first major campaign in India at Champaran, in northern Bihar, supporting farmers forced to grow indigo for British planters. It became a model for the larger struggles that followed.

text: Chennai, once called Madras, is the capital of [[@tamil-nadu-temples|Tamil Nadu]] and the largest city on India's south-east coast. It got its nickname because for centuries it was where people and goods entered South India. Ships docked at its harbour, the main railway lines south began there, and later its airport linked the region to the world.
About 1 crore people live in the wider city today. It is famous for its long beach, its ancient temples, its [[@made-cars|car factories]], its music and its films.

st.reveal: Chennai sits on the east coast, in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats during the summer monsoon. Its heaviest rain comes later, from the northeast monsoon and cyclones over the Bay of Bengal in October to December.

sec.t:
In 1639, two officers of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]], Francis Day and Andrew Cogan, got permission from a local ruler to build on a strip of sand. In 1640 they began building Fort St George, the first major English fort in India, and finished it a few years later. A town called George Town grew up beside it, near older Tamil villages such as Mylapore and Triplicane.

Mylapore was already ancient. Its Kapaleeshwarar Temple, dedicated to Shiva, has a tall gopuram, a gateway tower covered in hundreds of brightly painted figures. Today Fort St George houses Tamil Nadu's government and a museum.

sec.h: A gateway by sea, road and rail
sec.t:
Chennai's port became one of the busiest on the Bay of Bengal. Railways spread out from the city in the 1800s, and the routes to Bengaluru, Madurai and Kerala all start here. Today big car makers have factories nearby, and so many vehicles are made in the region that it is often called the Detroit of India, after the American car city.

Further down the coast, about 55 km away, lies [[@pallavas|Mahabalipuram]], with rock-cut temples carved by the Pallava kings around 1,300 years ago. It is a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

Walk through an old Chennai street at dawn and you will see kolams, patterns drawn in rice flour on doorsteps. Many families draw a fresh one every morning. Filter coffee, made by dripping hot water through ground coffee and mixing it with frothy milk, is poured between two steel cups to cool it. Tamil, the language of the city, is one of the oldest languages still spoken, with poems written more than 2,000 years ago. Signboards, films and politics in Chennai all show deep pride in it.

Marina Beach stretches for several kilometres along the city's edge and fills with families every evening. On 26 December 2004, a [[@tsunami|tsunami]] caused by an earthquake near Indonesia struck the coast. Waves swept across the beach and many people lost their lives along the Tamil Nadu coast. Warning systems have since been built across the Indian Ocean.

sec.h: Too much water, then too little
sec.t: Chennai has no big river feeding it all year, so it depends on lakes and rain. In 2015 heavy rain flooded large parts of the city. In 2019 the main [[reservoir|reservoirs]] nearly dried up and water had to be brought in by train. The city now recycles more water and takes salt out of seawater in desalination plants, trying to be ready for both extremes.

text: The Navajo Nation is the largest Native American reservation in the United States. It covers about 71,000 square kilometres of desert, canyons and mesas where Arizona, Utah and New Mexico meet. That is bigger than ten of the fifty US states, and a little larger than Sri Lanka.

The Navajo people call themselves the Diné, which means "the People". They are a sovereign nation, which means they govern themselves within the USA. They have their own elected president, a council, police, courts and flag. About 4 lakh people were enrolled as Navajo citizens in 2021, though many live outside the reservation. Navajo citizens are also American citizens, and they vote in US elections too.

st.reveal: The door of a traditional hogan faces east to greet the sunrise. Many families still keep a hogan for ceremonies, even if they live in a modern house next to it.

sec.t:
In Diné tradition, the homeland is bounded by four sacred mountains, one in each direction. The land inside holds famous places. [[@usa-wonder-monument-valley|Monument Valley]], with its tall red rock towers, is a Navajo tribal park that has appeared in countless Western films. Canyon de Chelly has cliffs streaked dark red, with ruins of old stone houses tucked into alcoves.

The traditional Navajo home is the hogan, a round or eight-sided house of logs and earth. Its doorway faces east, so the first thing to enter each morning is the rising sun. Many families still keep a hogan for ceremonies beside their modern house.

Life here can be hard. Many homes are far from shops and hospitals, and some estimates suggest about a third of households lack running water. Families often haul water in tanks from distant wells, so getting water to every home is one of the Nation's big goals.

sec.h: A language that won a war
sec.t:
The Navajo language, Diné bizaad, is complex, with tones and verbs that change in many ways. During the Second World War, the US Marines recruited Navajo men to send radio messages in a code built from their language. About 400 Navajo [[@code-talkers|code talkers]] served in the Pacific, and the enemy never broke their code.

For years the code was secret, and the men could not talk about it. They were honoured with medals by the US Congress in 2001.

Fewer children grow up speaking Navajo today, so schools and families work to keep it alive. In 2013, the original [[@star-wars-effect|Star Wars]] film was [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbed]] into Navajo, and audiences packed cinemas to hear it.

Sheep came to the region with the Spanish in the 1500s, and the Navajo became expert herders. Navajo weavers spin and dye the wool and weave rugs and blankets on upright looms. Each rug can take weeks or months, with bold patterns of zigzags and diamonds.

Navajo silversmiths make jewellery set with blue turquoise. And in a state that ignores daylight saving time, the Navajo Nation does change its clocks, so that it keeps the same time across its land in Arizona, Utah and New Mexico.

text: *Chandamama* was a monthly children's magazine full of [[@indian-folk-tales|folk tales]], myths, legends and moral stories, beautifully illustrated in colour. It was started in July 1947 in Madras, now [[@chennai|Chennai]], first in Telugu and Tamil. It soon appeared in more than ten Indian languages, as well as English from 1955.

Its name means "Uncle Moon", the friendly moon of Indian lullabies, such as "Chanda mama door ke". For decades it was one of the most-read [[@childrens-magazines|children's magazines]] in India. Families waited for each new issue, and children passed copies between houses until the pages fell apart. It finally stopped publishing in 2013, but many older Indians still remember its stories and pictures vividly.

They come from a much older collection, the Vetala Panchavimshati, "Twenty-five Tales of the Vetala". A version appears in Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara, written in Sanskrit in the 11th century.

sec.t:
Chandamama was founded by B. Nagi Reddy and his partner Chakrapani. Together they also ran Vijaya Vauhini Studios in Madras, one of the biggest film studios in South India, which made many Telugu and Tamil films in [[@cinema-south|South Indian cinema]].

They wanted a magazine that brought India's old stories to children in their own languages. Chakrapani shaped what went into it in its early years. The magazine printed stories from the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]] and [[@mahabharata|Mahabharata]], from the [[@panchatantra-tales|Panchatantra]] and Jataka tales, and folk tales from many regions, along with new stories in the same style.

Chandamama's most famous feature was the series about King Vikram and Betal, a ghostly spirit. Every story began the same way. On a dark, stormy night, the brave king climbs a tree in a cremation ground, lifts down a corpse in which Betal lives, and carries it over his shoulder.

As he walks, Betal tells him a story that ends with a puzzle about right and wrong. If Vikram knows the answer, he must speak. As soon as he does, Betal escapes and flies back to the tree. Next month, the whole thing starts again.

One riddle tells of three queens. The first faints when a lotus petal falls on her. The second gets blisters from moonlight. The third is bruised just by hearing a pestle pounding rice far away. Which queen is the most delicate? Vikram says the third, because the others were at least touched by something, and off flies Betal.

These tales are very old. They come from the *Vetala Panchavimshati*, "Twenty-five Tales of the Vetala", which appears in Somadeva's Sanskrit collection, the *Kathasaritsagara*, from the 11th century. Indian television also turned them into a popular series in the 1980s.

{{story:moon-phases}}

The magazine's pictures were as loved as its stories. Artists such as M. T. V. Acharya and K. C. Sivasankaran, known as Sankar, drew kings, sages, demons and village folk in rich colour.

Sankar drew the Vikram and Betal pictures for decades: the determined king, the grinning spirit, the twisted tree. He kept working for the magazine into old age and died in 2020, aged 97.

From the 1990s, children had more choices: cable television, comics like [[@tinkle|Tinkle]], and later the internet. Chandamama struggled to keep up. It was sold to a new owner in 2007, which tried to modernise it, but the business ran into money troubles and the magazine stopped in 2013.

Old issues are now collected and shared by fans, and many still turn up in family cupboards. For a generation of Indian children, the moon on the cover meant a new set of stories was waiting inside.

text: Dragons turn up in stories from China, India, Europe, the Middle East and the Americas, among peoples who never met. Nobody knows for certain why. Scholars point to a few likely reasons that may work together.

One is [[@fossils-form|fossils]]: ancient people dug up giant bones and skulls and tried to explain them. Another is fear. Humans have always feared snakes, big cats and birds of prey, and a dragon combines all three. A third is travel. Stories moved along trade routes, changing as they went, like a long game of telephone.

st.prompt: In old China, people ground up "dragon bones" as medicine. What were they really?
st.reveal: Scientists who examined "dragon bones" found fossil teeth and bones of extinct animals, from ancient horses to rhinos. To anyone who had never heard of fossils, giant buried bones looked like proof that monsters had lived.

n.certNote: Nobody can prove why so many cultures imagined dragons. Fossils, fear of real predators and stories spreading along trade routes are the main ideas, and each probably explains part of it.

sec.t:
A Chinese dragon, called long, is long and snaky, with whiskers, horns and four legs, and usually no wings. It lives in rivers, seas and clouds and brings rain for crops. It was the symbol of the emperor, and 2024 was a Year of the Dragon, considered a lucky year to be born. You can find many more in [[@myths-chinese|Chinese myths]].

A European dragon is heavier, with bat-like wings and fiery breath. It hoards treasure and fights heroes like St George, or the old warrior Beowulf in an English poem more than 1,000 years old. In the Christian art of Europe, it often stood for evil.

So the same word covers creatures that are almost opposites. When early European travellers wrote about Chinese dragons, they translated long as "dragon", and the mix-up has stuck ever since.

sec.h: Serpents of India and the Americas

sec.t:
The historian Adrienne Mayor has argued that [[fossil|fossils]] shaped many monster stories. In China, "dragon bones" were ground up as medicine for centuries. When scientists examined them in the early 1900s, they turned out to be fossil teeth and bones. A trail of such teeth helped lead researchers to a cave near Beijing, where they found Peking Man, an early human about 750,000 years old (estimates vary).

Dinosaur bones lie exposed in deserts from Mongolia to the American West. Seeing a skull as long as a bicycle, who would not think of dragons?

The anthropologist David E. Jones suggested another idea. Our early ancestors were hunted by three main killers: snakes, leopards and eagles. Our brains learned to react to them quickly. A dragon has a snake's body, a big cat's claws and a bird's wings, almost a mash-up of everything our ancestors feared.

Real animals may have helped too. [[@crocodiles-alligators|Crocodiles]] are scaly, have huge jaws and lurk in rivers, just like many water dragons.

Dragons are still proud national symbols. The flag of Wales has a red dragon. The kingdom of [[@bhutan|Bhutan]] calls itself Druk Yul, the Land of the Thunder Dragon, and a white dragon stretches across its flag.

And there is one real dragon. On a few Indonesian islands lives the Komodo dragon, a lizard up to about 3 metres long, close to the length of a small car. It does not breathe fire, but its bite carries [[venom|venom]], and it can eat a deer. The strangest twist is that it is a cousin, distant but real, of the little [[@lizards|lizards]] that chase insects on your wall at home.

text: Giants turn up in stories nearly everywhere. Greece had Titans and the one-eyed Cyclopes. Norse myth had frost giants. India has Kumbhakarna, who slept for months at a time, and the rakshasa Hidimba from the Mahabharata. The Bible has Goliath. America has Paul Bunyan, a lumberjack so big his footprints made lakes.

Nobody knows for sure why. Historians and psychologists point to a few likely reasons. People found enormous bones in the ground. They saw landscapes and ruins that looked too big for humans to have made. And every child spends years looking up at adults who seem huge and powerful. Giants turn all that into a story.

n.certNote: Nobody can prove where any particular giant story came from. The fossil idea is supported by some historians and doubted by others, and psychology and the urge to explain big landscapes are other possible reasons.

sec.t:
Picture a farmer in ancient Greece breaking ground and hitting a skull the size of a cart wheel. On islands like Crete and Sicily, people did find skulls of [[extinct|extinct]] dwarf elephants. An elephant skull has a big hole in the middle of the face where the trunk joins. It looks like one huge eye socket.

In 1914, a scientist named Othenio Abel suggested these skulls inspired the [[@greek-myths|Cyclopes]]. In 2000, the historian Adrienne Mayor went further in her book *The First Fossil Hunters*. She argued that Greeks and Romans collected giant bones and treated them as remains of heroes and monsters. Not everyone agrees, but bones of [[@mammoths|mammoths]] and other big animals were certainly found and displayed in ancient temples.

In many myths, giants were there first. Norse stories say the world was built from the body of the frost giant Ymir. His flesh became land, his bones became mountains and his skull became the sky. In Greek myth, the Titans ruled before Zeus and the Olympian gods overthrew them.

Giants in these stories stand for wild, old forces like frost, fire and storms. The gods who defeat them bring order. You can read it as a story about people taming a dangerous world.

In the [[@ramayana|Ramayana]], Ravana's brother Kumbhakarna was so large that waking him took an army. In one telling, soldiers blew conches, beat drums and drove elephants over him. He slept for six months, woke for a single day to eat mountains of food, then slept again. When he finally joined the battle, he was fierce but also honest. He told Ravana he was wrong to kidnap Sita, and fought anyway out of loyalty.

Many giants are like that: frightening, but with a sad or funny side. In the Mahabharata, the rakshasi Hidimbi falls in love with the hero Bhima, and their son Ghatotkacha grows into a giant warrior who fights on the side of the Pandavas.

Giants keep appearing in new stories, from Roald Dahl's *The BFG* to the Titans in *Attack on Titan*. Psychologists note that small children live in a land of giants. Adults are two or three times their height and control almost everything.

A giant can be a bully like Goliath or a gentle friend like the BFG. And giants have company. Almost every culture also tells of [[@myths-dragons|dragons]], and some historians think the same buried bones lie behind those stories too.

text: Slang is the informal, playful language of a group: teenagers, soldiers, musicians, gamers, a school or a city neighbourhood. It comes from the same urge that makes friends invent nicknames and [[@life-handshake|secret handshakes]]. [[@words-made-up|New words]] mark who belongs, add fun, and say things that ordinary words can't quite capture.

Slang words are made by shortening, mixing, borrowing and twisting older words. Most vanish within a few years. A few survive so long that they become ordinary language, and nobody remembers they were ever slang. "Mob", "bus" and "OK" all started out that way.

myth: Slang is just lazy or bad language.
Slang follows its own patterns and takes real creativity. Linguists study it closely, and many ordinary words, like "bus" and "mob", started life as slang that people once complained about.

sec.h: The joke that conquered the world
sec.t:
In the 1830s, Boston newspapers had a craze for jokey abbreviations of misspelled phrases. "O.W." stood for "oll wright" and "K.Y." for "know yuse". In March 1839, the *Boston Morning Post* printed "O.K." for "oll korrect", a silly spelling of "all correct".

Most of these jokes died quickly. OK survived, helped by the 1840 US presidential election. Supporters of President Martin Van Buren, nicknamed "Old Kinderhook" after his home town, formed "O.K. Clubs". The American scholar Allen Walker Read tracked down this history in the 1960s. Today people say "OK" in Hindi, Japanese, Swahili and dozens of other languages.

Slang has a toolkit. Shortening turns "fabulous" into "fab" and "information" into "info". Blending squashes words together. Changing meaning makes "sick" or "wicked" mean excellent. Borrowing pulls in words from other languages and other groups.

Some slang is meant to hide meaning from outsiders. In Cockney rhyming slang, from East London, you replace a word with a phrase that rhymes with it, and then often drop the rhyming part. "Apples and pears" means stairs. "Use your loaf" means use your head, because "loaf of bread" rhymes with head. Traders and street sellers could talk in front of strangers without being understood.

Soldiers have always been busy slang makers too. British soldiers who served in India took home the word "Blighty", meaning Britain. It came from the Hindustani *vilayati*, meaning foreign, and was used most widely during the [[@world-war-one|First World War]].

Social media now spreads slang faster than ever. A word can start in one online community, travel worldwide in weeks and sound old-fashioned within a year. Oxford Languages named "rizz", meaning charm or the ability to attract someone, its Word of the Year for 2023. The word grew from the end of "charisma" and spread through online videos.

[[@dictionaries|Dictionaries]] wait to see whether a slang word lasts before adding it. Many don't. In 1710, the writer Jonathan Swift complained that "mob", short for the Latin *mobile vulgus*, was a lazy new word that was ruining English. Today nobody blinks at it, and some of the slang that annoys your parents may turn up in your grandchildren's textbooks.

text: Lentils are eaten almost everywhere, but they matter most in South Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and southern Europe. They are small, lens-shaped seeds from a bushy plant in the pea family. In fact, the glass lens got its name from the lentil, because early lenses had the same shape.

India eats more lentils than any other country. Red masoor dal simmers in kitchens from Kolkata to Lahore. In Lebanon, people eat lentils with rice and crispy onions. In Ethiopia, red lentils become a spicy stew. In France and Italy, small green lentils go into soups and salads. And Canada, which grows the most, eats only a small part of its harvest.

st.prompt: Which of these Indian dals is actually made from lentils?
st.reveal: Masoor is the lentil, Lens culinaris, in its red split form or whole brown form. Toor comes from pigeon peas and chana dal from a small chickpea. In India, "dal" means any split pulse, and lentils are just one of them.

sec.t:
Lentils were among the very first plants people farmed. Seeds found at early farming villages in the Middle East show that lentils were being grown around 9,000 to 10,000 years ago, alongside wheat, barley, peas and chickpeas. The crop spread to Egypt, Greece, India and beyond.

Lentils show up in old stories too. In the Bible, Esau sells his birthright to his brother Jacob for a bowl of red lentil stew. Lentils have also been found in ancient Egyptian tombs, buried with food for the afterlife.

sec.h: A plant that feeds the soil
sec.t:
Lentils belong to the [[legume|legume]] family, like peas and beans. Their roots carry tiny lumps filled with [[bacteria|bacteria]] that can take nitrogen from the air and turn it into a form plants can use. When the plants die back, some of that nitrogen stays behind, helping the next crop.

That is why farmers often grow lentils in turns with wheat. It makes the [[@soil-made|soil]] richer without as much fertiliser.

In India and Pakistan, masoor dal is cooked with turmeric, then finished with a tadka of hot ghee or oil, cumin, garlic and chilli. In the Middle East, mujaddara mixes lentils, rice and deeply browned onions. Egypt's famous street food koshari piles lentils, rice, pasta and tomato sauce into one bowl.

In [[@ethiopia|Ethiopia]], misir wot is a red lentil stew flavoured with a spice blend called berbere, eaten with spongy injera bread. France grows small green lentils around Le Puy, a variety protected by law, a bit like Darjeeling tea. In Italy, lentils with sausage are a New Year's Eve tradition, eaten for luck and wealth.

About a quarter of a dry lentil's weight is [[protein|protein]], which is why lentils are so important in [[@vegetarian|vegetarian]] diets. They also have fibre, iron and folate. Dal and rice together give a good mix of the building blocks the body needs.

Unlike kidney beans or chickpeas, lentils don't need soaking and cook in about 20 to 30 minutes. The UN named 2016 the International Year of Pulses to encourage people to eat more of them. They are cheap, they keep for months in a jar, and they don't need much water to grow.
